title: 〜のやら (I wonder ...)
meaning: The speaker is puzzled or unsure about something and muses aloud with doubt, worry, or resignation: "I wonder ..."
connection: (question word) + verb/i-adjective plain form / na-adjective or noun + な + のやら

senses.label: I wonder ...
senses.meaning: Used at the end of a sentence as a self-directed question. Usually pairs with question words like 「何」, 「どこ」, 「いつ」, 「どう」. Carries worry, resignation, or mild annoyance.
senses.connection: Question word + plain form + のやら (どこへ行ったのやら, 何を考えているのやら)
examples: Where on earth did that kid go, I wonder.
I have no idea what he's thinking.
Who knows when this construction will ever finish.

senses.label: Inserted clause
senses.meaning: 「〜のやら」 plus a comma works as an aside: "Who knows how, but ..." The following clause states what actually happened.
senses.connection: Question word + plain form + のやら、+ main clause
examples: Who knows where she heard it, but my mother already knew about my marriage.
Who knows who started it, but that rumor is spreading.

senses.label: ... or ...?
senses.meaning: 「〜のやら〜のやら」 sets two possibilities side by side: "Is it A or B? I can't tell." Often used when someone's attitude is ambiguous.
senses.connection: Plain form + のやら + plain form + のやら
examples: I can't tell from his face whether he's happy or angry.

notes: In speech it often becomes 「〜んやら」, as in 「何がしたいんやら」.
「のやら」 is a question to yourself. It is not used to ask the listener directly.
「何やら」 ("something or other") and 「どうやら」 ("apparently") are adverbs, not this pattern.

daily.title: Looking for something
daily.description: Mom mutters while hunting for her keys.
daily.example: Where did I put my keys? I can't remember at all.

daily.title: Worried about a child
daily.description: A child is out late, and the parents talk to themselves.
daily.example: What could he be doing out at this hour?

daily.title: Reading a novel
daily.description: A character feels helpless about the situation.
daily.example: I can't even guess what will happen from here on.

work.title: Grumbling with a coworker
work.description: Frustration with a boss who keeps changing plans. Only among close colleagues.
work.example: What does the manager even want? The policy changed again.

etymology: Formed from the nominalizer 「の」 plus the uncertainty particle 「やら」. 「やら」 is usually traced to a contraction of 「にやあらん」 ("might it be ...?"), so it carries a sense of uncertainty in itself.

similar.title: 〜のやら・〜ものやら・〜ことやら
similar.explanation: Same meaning. 「〜ものやら」 and 「〜ことやら」 feel more exclamatory (どうしたものやら, 何のことやら). This entry covers the most common form, 「〜のやら」.

similar.title: 〜のやら〜のやら
similar.explanation: 「〜のやら〜のやら」 specifically lists two possibilities you can't tell apart. A single 「〜のやら」 means you're puzzled about one thing.

similar.title: 〜かな
similar.explanation: 「〜かな」 is a light, neutral question to yourself. 「〜のやら」 adds a sense of "I just can't figure it out" with resignation or worry.

similar.title: 〜やら〜やら
similar.explanation: 「AやらBやら」 lists things ("A and B and so on") with no question meaning. 「〜のやら」 expresses puzzlement.

title: 〜に〜て／〜に〜た (repetition for emphasis)
meaning: The same verb is repeated to show an action done over and over, to the extreme: "... and ... again," "... with all one's might."
connection: Verb masu-stem + に + same verb in te-form / ta-form

senses.label: ... over and over
senses.meaning: 「〜に〜て」 links to the next clause. It stresses a long, thorough process that leads to the result. Common: 「考えに考えて」, 「悩みに悩んで」, 「迷いに迷って」.
senses.connection: Verb masu-stem + に + same verb te-form (考えに考えて, 走りに走って)
examples: After thinking it over and over, I decided to quit my job.
This is a conclusion I reached after agonizing over it.
I ran and ran all the way to the station and just made the last train.

senses.label: Extremely ...
senses.meaning: 「〜に〜た」 ends a sentence or modifies a noun to show an extreme degree. 「待ちに待った」 ("long-awaited") is a set phrase.
senses.connection: Verb masu-stem + に + same verb ta-form (待ちに待った + noun, 泣きに泣いた)
examples: The long-awaited summer vacation has arrived.
That night, she cried and cried.
The carefully refined proposal was finally accepted.

notes: Both parts must be the same verb: 「考えに考える」 is fine, but not 「考えに悩む」.
Mostly used to narrate past experiences with emotion. It has a written or storytelling tone.
In 「買いに行く」 or 「食べに来る」, 「に」 marks purpose and the next verb is different. That is not this pattern.

daily.title: The big day arrives
daily.description: A child's long-awaited trip is finally here.
daily.example: The long-awaited day of our trip has finally come!

daily.title: Explaining your choice
daily.description: Telling a friend you decided after a lot of hesitation.
daily.example: I went back and forth for ages and finally chose this university.

daily.title: Reading a novel
daily.description: A scene of a character in deep grief.
daily.example: The boy who had lost his mother cried and cried all night.

work.title: Product launch
work.description: The person in charge presents a carefully polished new product.
work.example: Let me introduce a new product our development team has refined again and again.

work.title: News report
work.description: A report on negotiations that dragged on.
work.example: After a long and bitter dispute, the negotiations finally reached an agreement.

etymology: 「に」 originally marked purpose or addition: "in order to ..." or "on top of ...". Stacking the same verb means adding the same action again and again, which gives the sense of "repeatedly, to the extreme."

similar.title: 〜に〜を重ねて
similar.explanation: 「〜に〜を重ねて」 repeats a noun (努力に努力を重ねて). 「〜に〜て」 repeats a verb (考えに考えて). Both mean repeated, accumulated effort.

similar.title: 〜抜く
similar.explanation: 「考え抜く」 stresses seeing it through to the end. 「考えに考える」 stresses many rounds and a hard process, with stronger emotion.

similar.title: 〜てばかりいる
similar.explanation: 「泣いてばかりいる」 means "always crying," often critical. 「泣きに泣いた」 means one episode of intense crying, said with emotion.

title: 〜に〜に (listing)
meaning: Uses 「に」 to pile up items one after another: "A, B, and C too," stressing that there are many things.

senses.label: One thing after another
senses.meaning: Lists tasks you're juggling at once, stressing how busy you are. Common: 「〜に〜にと忙しい」, 「〜に〜に追われる」.
senses.connection: Noun + に + noun + にと + 忙しい／追われる
examples: Between studying and club activities, I lead a busy life.
Between work, housework, and childcare, I have no time for myself.

senses.label: Item after item
senses.meaning: Adds items one by one: "A, plus B, plus C." Often used for food or things that go together.
senses.connection: Noun + に + noun + に + noun
examples: Beer, edamame, and yakitori: there's no greater happiness.
The table was lined with treats like sushi and tempura.

notes: A 「と」 often follows the last item, giving 「〜に〜にと」, followed by a predicate like 「忙しい」.
Compared with 「〜や〜」, 「〜に〜に」 feels like stacking items one on top of another, stressing quantity.
Don't confuse it with 「に」 for places or targets. 「東京に大阪に行く」 is unnatural; say 「東京と大阪に行く」.

daily.title: Talking about student life
daily.description: A college student tells a relative how things are going.
daily.example: Between classes, my part-time job, and my club, I'm rushing around every day.

daily.title: Ordering at a get-together
daily.description: A friend excitedly orders a pile of dishes at an izakaya.
daily.example: Fried chicken, fries, sashimi: let's just order it all.

work.title: Employee interview
work.description: A working mom talks about balancing work and family in the company newsletter.
work.example: Between work and raising kids, every day is one challenge after another.

etymology: 「に」 has a sense of "adding" (as in 「AにBを加える」). Linking nouns with 「に」 one after another produces the listing meaning "and on top of that ...".

similar.title: 〜や〜など
similar.explanation: 「〜や〜など」 just gives a few examples in a neutral tone. 「〜に〜に」 stresses adding item after item, highlighting abundance or busyness.

similar.title: 〜やら〜やら
similar.explanation: 「〜やら〜やら」 also lists, but often feels chaotic and overwhelming. 「〜に〜に」 also works in positive contexts (ごちそう).

similar.title: 〜だの〜だの
similar.explanation: 「〜だの〜だの」 mostly lists other people's complaints or demands, with annoyance. 「〜に〜に」 has no such negative tone.

title: 〜や〜 (just one or two)
meaning: 「一〜や二〜」 means "just one or two," stressing a small number that is nothing unusual or not worth worrying about.
connection: 一 + counter + や + 二 + counter (一度や二度, 一人や二人)

senses.label: Just one or two
senses.meaning: "One or two is normal, nothing special." Often followed by 「は（誰にでも）ある」 or 「くらい」. Used to comfort or show tolerance.
senses.connection: Noun の + 一つや二つ／一度や二度 + は
examples: Everyone fails once or twice.
It's only natural to have a flaw or two.
You'll make a friend or two in no time.

senses.label: More than once or twice
senses.meaning: With the negative 「〜ではない」, it means "far more than once or twice," stressing how often. Often carries frustration or emotion.
senses.connection: 一度や二度／一回や二回 + ではない
examples: This isn't the first or second time he's been late.
We've had this kind of complaint many more times than once or twice.

senses.label: Even that much is fine
senses.meaning: "That small amount is nothing." Followed by "it's fine," "I don't mind," and so on.
senses.connection: 一日や二日／一万円や二万円 + ても／くらい
examples: I'm fine even if I don't sleep for a day or two.
If it's ten or twenty thousand yen, I'll lend it to you.

notes: The noun before it often takes 「の」: 「失敗の一度や二度」, 「欠点の一つや二つ」.
It must be "one" and "two" together to mean "a few." The actual number doesn't matter.
The negative 「〜ではない」 means the opposite: "a lot." Watch the context.

daily.title: Comforting a friend
daily.description: Your friend is down after failing an exam.
daily.example: Don't get discouraged over failing once or twice.

daily.title: Complaining about family
daily.description: A wife is fed up with her husband forgetting things.
daily.example: This isn't the first time you've forgotten a promise, is it?

work.title: A boss encouraging a new hire
work.description: A boss talks to a new employee who made a mistake.
work.example: Don't worry about a mistake or two.

work.title: Customer complaint meeting
work.description: The person in charge stresses that the problem isn't a one-off.
work.example: We have received similar complaints more than just once or twice.

etymology: 「や」 is a listing particle. Pairing the two smallest numbers, 「一」 and 「二」, means "a tiny amount like one or two," which leads to the nuance "nothing unusual, not worth mentioning."

similar.title: 〜たりとも
similar.explanation: 「一円たりとも」 stresses "not even one" and takes a negative. 「一つや二つ」 stresses "one or two is fine, perfectly normal."

similar.title: 〜や〜など
similar.explanation: 「〜や〜など」 is ordinary listing. This entry is the fixed pattern 「一〜や二〜」 meaning a small amount.

similar.title: 〜として〜ない（一人として）
similar.explanation: 「一人として来なかった」 means "not a single person came," a total negation. 「一人や二人」 means "there's bound to be one or two."

title: 〜よう (manner / way)
meaning: Attaches to the verb masu-stem to make a noun meaning the "way something looks / its degree" or the "way of doing something."

senses.label: The way someone looks
senses.meaning: Shows how a state shows itself and to what degree, usually a strong emotion or reaction. Common: 「〜ようといったら」, 「大変な〜ようだ」.
senses.connection: Verb masu-stem + よう (喜びよう, 慌てよう, 落ち込みよう)
examples: You should have seen how happy he was when he found out he passed.
She was so depressed it was painful to watch.
Seeing how angry my father was, I realized how serious it was.

senses.label: The way of doing
senses.meaning: Shows a method or way. Common: 「ものは言いようだ」 ("it's all in how you say it"), 「考えようによっては」 ("depending on how you look at it"), 「やりようはある」 ("there's always a way").
senses.connection: Verb masu-stem + よう + は／によって（は）／だ (言いよう, 考えよう, やりよう)
examples: It's all in how you say it; the way you phrase things changes how others take it.
Depending on how you look at it, this failure is also a good experience.
Even without time, there are plenty of ways to do it.

notes: Don't confuse it with the volitional form: 「食べよう」 and 「考えよう」 can also mean "let's eat / let's think." Check whether 「は／によって／といったら」 follows.
「〜ようがない」 ("there's no way to ...") grew out of this usage but is now a separate pattern.
「〜ようだ」 ("seems") follows the plain form. 「行くようだ」 and 「行きよう」 connect differently.

daily.title: Describing a family member's reaction
daily.description: Telling a friend how your child reacted to a present.
daily.example: Seeing how happy my son was, I was glad I bought it.

daily.title: Telling a friend to lighten up
daily.description: A friend frets over something small, and you suggest another angle.
daily.example: Well, it all depends on how you look at it.

daily.title: Reading a novel
daily.description: A character is described panicking.
daily.example: From how flustered he was, it was clear he was hiding something.

work.title: Discussing solutions
work.description: A project hits trouble, and a senior colleague encourages the team.
work.example: Even with a small budget, there must be a way.

work.title: A reminder about wording
work.description: A boss reminds a team member to watch their wording when replying to a client.
work.example: Even the same content can cause friction depending on how you say it.

etymology: 「よう」 is written 「様」 and originally means "appearance, form." After a verb's continuative form (masu-stem), it means "how the action looks," and by extension "the way of doing it."

similar.title: 〜方（かた）
similar.explanation: 「読み方」 is an objective method or procedure. 「読みよう」 leans toward "how you view or handle it," often implying the result depends on your view.

similar.title: 〜ようがない
similar.explanation: 「〜ようがない」 means "there's no way to ...," the negative set phrase of this usage. This entry covers the positive or neutral "way, manner."

similar.title: 〜ぶり
similar.explanation: 「仕事ぶり」 and 「話しぶり」 attach to nouns or masu-stems and describe an objective manner. 「〜よう」 emphasizes an extreme degree (喜びよう).

title: 〜もしない (not even ...)
meaning: Adds 「も」 to the verb masu-stem and negates it, stressing "not even (this basic thing)." Often shows annoyance, surprise, or the unexpected.
connection: Verb masu-stem + もしない／もしなかった

senses.label: Not even ...
senses.meaning: Stresses that someone doesn't do even the most basic action. Usually shows the speaker's annoyance or blame. Common: 「見向きもしない」, 「振り向きもしない」, 「読みもしない」.
senses.connection: Verb masu-stem + もしない (見向きもしない, 返事もしない, 見もしない)
examples: He won't even pay attention to what I say.
He threw away the letter I worked so hard on without even reading it.
Even when I called him, my son didn't so much as turn around.

senses.label: Never even imagined
senses.meaning: 「思いもしなかった」, 「考えもしなかった」, 「予想もしなかった」 mean something was completely unexpected. The tone is surprise, not blame.
senses.connection: 思い／考え／予想 + もしなかった
examples: I never dreamed I'd actually win.
I never imagined it would turn out like this.

senses.label: Nonexistent
senses.meaning: 「ありもしない」 and 「できもしない」 modify nouns: "that doesn't exist at all / that can't be done at all." Used to criticize made-up stories or empty promises.
senses.connection: ありもしない／できもしない + noun
examples: I'm troubled because someone is spreading groundless rumors about me.
You shouldn't make promises you can't keep.

notes: In 「何もしない」 and 「誰もしない」, 「も」 follows a question word for total negation. That is not this pattern.
「勉強もしない」 is noun + も + しない ("doesn't even study"). Similar meaning, different structure.
The written form is 「〜もせず（に）」, as in 「見向きもせずに通り過ぎた」.

daily.title: Complaining about a child
daily.description: Mom complains her kid ignored the meal she worked hard on.
daily.example: I went to the trouble of cooking, and he left without even eating.

daily.title: Telling a friend about a surprise
daily.description: A friend throws you a surprise birthday party.
daily.example: I never imagined a surprise like this!

daily.title: When falsely accused
daily.description: Misunderstood by a classmate, you vent to a friend.
daily.example: I can't believe I'm being blamed for something I didn't even do.

work.title: News report
work.description: A report says executives ignored a problem.
work.example: The management didn't even listen to the employees' complaints.

work.title: Project review
work.description: Explaining an unexpected problem at a post-mortem.
work.example: No one anticipated this kind of trouble.

etymology: Built from verb masu-stem (continuative form) + the particle 「も」 + 「しない」. Here 「も」 means "even," singling out the action itself and negating it, which creates the emphasis "not even the most basic thing."

similar.title: 〜もしないで
similar.explanation: 「〜もしないで」 is followed by another action (読みもしないで捨てた): "did ... without even ...". 「〜もしない」 ends the sentence on its own.

similar.title: 〜やしない
similar.explanation: 「〜やしない」 is an intensified negative: "not ... at all." 「〜もしない」 adds "not even," highlighting that the most basic thing wasn't done.

similar.title: 〜さえ
similar.explanation: 「見さえしない」 is close to 「見もしない」, but 「さえ」 stresses an extreme example and sounds stronger.

meaning: A colloquial, emphatic negative: "not ... at all," "no way ...". Also appears in set forms like 「〜やしないか」 ("I'm worried that ...") and 「〜ったらありゃしない」 ("incredibly ...").
connection: Verb masu-stem + やしない; verb te-form + やしない; i-adjective + ったらありゃしない

senses.label: Not ... at all
senses.meaning: A strong negative with annoyance, scorn, or finality. Much more emotional than 「〜ない」. Casual speech between people who know each other.
senses.connection: Verb masu-stem + やしない (わかりやしない, できやしない, 来やしない)
examples: No matter how long you wait, he's not going to come.
With handwriting like this, nobody can read it.
An explanation like that won't make sense to anyone.

senses.label: I'm afraid that ...
senses.meaning: 「〜やしないか」 expresses worry that something bad might happen, like 「〜のではないか」. Often followed by 「と心配だ」 or 「とひやひやする」.
senses.connection: Verb masu-stem + やしないか (と心配だ)
examples: I'm worried my kid might catch a cold.
I was on edge the whole way, afraid it might rain.

senses.label: Incredibly ...
senses.meaning: 「〜ったらありゃしない」 means an extreme degree, "so ... it's unbearable," usually about something annoying. 「ありゃしない」 is a sound change of 「ありはしない」.
senses.connection: i-adjective / na-adjective + ったらありゃしない
examples: The construction next door is incredibly noisy.
The packed trains every morning are such a pain.

notes: 「やしない」 comes from 「はしない」 by sound change. It is very colloquial and not for formal situations.
The past is 「〜やしなかった」, the polite form is 「〜やしません」. A rough, masculine version is 「〜やしねえ」.
「〜てやしない」 follows the te-form, as in 「全然聞いてやしない」 ("not listening at all").

daily.title: Complaining about family
daily.description: Mom complains her kid never listens.
daily.example: No matter how many times I tell him, he doesn't listen at all.

daily.title: Worried about a trip
daily.description: Family members worry about the weather before a trip.
daily.example: I'm worried a typhoon might come.

daily.title: Complaining about the weather
daily.description: Grumbling to a friend in midsummer.
daily.example: This summer is unbearably hot.

work.title: Grumbling with a coworker
work.description: A coworker complains the system is hard to use. Only among close colleagues.
work.example: This system is such a pain to use.

etymology: The original form is verb masu-stem + the particle 「は」 + 「しない」, where 「は」 singles out the action for negation. In speech, 「は（wa）」 blended with the preceding vowel and became 「や」. 「ありゃしない」 is likewise a sound change of 「ありはしない」.

similar.title: 〜やしない・〜はしない
similar.explanation: That entry focuses on the written, determined use of 「〜はしない」. This one focuses on colloquial 「〜やしない」 and set forms like 「〜やしないか」 and 「〜ったらありゃしない」.

similar.title: 〜っこない
similar.explanation: 「〜っこない」 only means "impossible" (できっこない). 「〜やしない」 can also express annoyance that someone simply doesn't do something.

similar.title: 〜のではないか
similar.explanation: Both 「〜やしないか」 and 「〜のではないか」 express worry. 「〜やしないか」 is more colloquial and sounds more anxious.

meaning: The attributive form of the classical negative auxiliary 「ず」. It follows the verb's irrealis (nai) stem to modify a noun: "that does not ...". Solemn and literary.
connection: Verb nai-form minus ない + ざる + noun (する → せざる)

senses.label: Un-... + noun
senses.meaning: Like 「〜ない + noun」, but more solemn and literary. Common: 「知られざる」, 「見えざる」, 「招かれざる客」, 「予期せざる」.
senses.connection: Verb irrealis stem + ざる + noun (知られざる真実, 見えざる手)
examples: This book portrays the author's unknown past.
It is said that an "invisible hand" is at work in the market.
He was treated like an uninvited guest.

senses.label: One who does not / something that is not
senses.meaning: Followed by 「者」, 「こと」, or 「もの」: "a person / thing that does not ...". Found in proverbs, sayings, and solemn writing.
senses.connection: Verb irrealis stem + ざる + 者／こと／もの
examples: He who does not work shall not eat.
That is something that can never be forgiven.

senses.label: Set expressions
senses.meaning: Some forms are fixed phrases: 「絶えざる」 ("ceaseless"), 「たゆまざる」 ("untiring"), 「少なからざる」 ("considerable"), 「欠くべからざる」 ("indispensable").
senses.connection: 絶えざる／たゆまざる／少なからざる + noun
examples: Success is the result of ceaseless effort.
This accident had a considerable impact on society.

notes: For 「する」 the form is 「せざる」, as in 「予期せざる事態」.
「〜ざるを得ない」 ("have no choice but to") is a separate pattern. This entry covers noun modification.
The 「ざる」 in 「ざるそば」 and 「竹ざる」 means "bamboo basket" and is unrelated.

daily.title: Watching a documentary
daily.description: A documentary title promises little-known history.
daily.example: Uncovering the hidden face of the Warring States period.

daily.title: Reading a novel
daily.description: A novel describes an unseen force.
daily.example: I felt as though some invisible force was guiding me.

work.title: Company speech
work.description: The president thanks employees at a year-end event for their tireless work.
work.example: I thank you all for your untiring efforts.

work.title: News report
work.description: A report on a sudden incident.
work.example: The government is scrambling to deal with an unforeseen situation.

etymology: The classical negative auxiliary 「ず」 had two conjugation sets. One, the 「ざり」 series, came from 「ず + あり」 merging, and its attributive form is 「ざる」. Modern Japanese keeps it only in writing and set phrases.

similar.title: 〜ざる (+ noun)
similar.explanation: Both entries cover 「ざる」 modifying nouns. This one adds N1-level sayings and set phrases like 「〜ざる者」, 「絶えざる」, 「少なからざる」.

similar.title: 〜ざるを得ない
similar.explanation: 「〜ざるを得ない」 is a fixed pattern meaning "have no choice but to." 「〜ざる」 here modifies a noun: "that does not ...".

similar.title: 〜ぬ (negative)
similar.explanation: 「知らぬ人」 and 「知られざる」 are both classical negatives modifying nouns. 「〜ぬ」 is more common and slightly lighter; 「〜ざる」 is more solemn.

similar.title: 〜べからず／〜べからざる
similar.explanation: 「〜べからざる」 means "must not / should not be ...". Plain 「〜ざる」 just means "that does not ..." with no sense of obligation.

meaning: "Whatever ... may be": sets one factor aside and then states a judgment or attitude it doesn't affect.
connection: Noun + はどうあれ／がどうあれ

senses.label: Whatever the reason
senses.meaning: Sets aside the reason, motive, or process, then gives the speaker's criticism or judgment. Common: 「理由はどうあれ」, 「事情はどうあれ」, 「動機はどうあれ」.
senses.connection: 理由／事情／動機／経緯 + はどうあれ
examples: Whatever the reason, violence is unacceptable.
Whatever the circumstances, you're the one who broke the promise.

senses.label: Whatever the result
senses.meaning: Regardless of the result, the form, or others' opinions, the speaker gives a positive view, resolve, or evaluation. Common: 「結果はどうあれ」, 「形はどうあれ」.
senses.connection: 結果／形／周り + はどうあれ／がどうあれ
examples: Whatever the result, you did great sticking with it to the end.
Whatever others think of me, I'll go my own way.
Whatever form it takes, it's enough if your feelings come across.

notes: 「どうあれ」 is a shortened form of 「どうであれ」; both are fine. A more formal version is 「どうであろうと」.
The second half is usually the speaker's claim, judgment, or resolve, not a neutral statement of fact.
Don't confuse it with 「どうあれば（いい）」 ("how should it be?"), which is a conditional form.

daily.title: Breaking up a kids' fight
daily.description: A parent speaks to children who were fighting.
daily.example: Whatever the reason, whoever hit first is in the wrong.

daily.title: Encouraging a test-taker
daily.description: After an exam, family members comfort the child.
daily.example: Whatever the result, you did really well.

work.title: Handling a complaint
work.description: A manager stresses to the team that apologizing comes first.
work.example: Whatever happened, we should first apologize to the customer.

work.title: News commentary
work.description: A commentator evaluates a policy.
work.example: Whatever the motives, the direction of the reform deserves credit.

etymology: Made from the adverb 「どう」 ("how") and 「あれ」, the classical imperative of 「ある」, originally meaning "however it may be." The imperative here expresses concession, the same idea as 「何はともあれ」 and 「いずれにせよ」.

similar.title: 〜はともかく
similar.explanation: 「〜はともかく」 means "setting ... aside," hinting that something else matters more. 「〜はどうあれ」 stresses that "whatever ... is, it doesn't change the judgment."

similar.title: 〜であれ
similar.explanation: 「〜であれ」 follows concrete nouns or question words (誰であれ, 何であれ). 「〜はどうあれ」 follows abstract nouns like 「理由」 and 「結果」.

similar.title: 〜いかんにかかわらず
similar.explanation: 「〜いかんにかかわらず」 is more formal, common in rules and official documents. 「〜はどうあれ」 leans toward expressing the speaker's attitude.

similar.title: 〜にしろ・〜にせよ
similar.explanation: 「〜にしろ」 can follow various clauses to concede a point. 「〜はどうあれ」 is a fixed "noun + はどうあれ" pattern.

title: 〜れる・〜られる (spontaneous)
meaning: Attached to verbs of thinking, feeling, or emotion, it shows a feeling or thought arising on its own: "can't help ...," "naturally ...". (spontaneous form)
connection: Godan verb nai-stem + れる; ichidan verb + られる (思われる, 感じられる, 偲ばれる)

senses.label: Naturally recalled
senses.meaning: Seeing something brings a memory or feeling to mind on its own. The subject is often the thing recalled, marked with 「が」. Common: 「思い出される」, 「感じられる」, 「偲ばれる」.
senses.connection: Noun + が + 思い出される／感じられる／偲ばれる
examples: Whenever I see this photo, my childhood comes back to me.
In the chill of the wind, you can sense autumn coming.
This letter brings my grandfather's character to mind.

senses.label: Emotions welling up
senses.meaning: Worry, regret, anticipation, and so on arise involuntarily. Common: 「案じられる」, 「悔やまれる」, 「待たれる」. Reserved and written in tone.
senses.connection: Noun + が + 案じられる／悔やまれる／待たれる
examples: I can't help worrying about the health of my daughter, who has started living alone.
I still regret the decision I made back then.
Everyone is eagerly awaiting the new drug's approval.

senses.label: Softened judgment
senses.meaning: 「〜と思われる」 and 「〜と考えられる」 mean "it would seem / it is thought that ...", making a personal judgment sound objective and indirect. Common in news and academic papers.
senses.connection: Plain form + と思われる／と考えられる
examples: It seems that problems still remain with this plan.
The cause of the accident is thought to be a brake failure.

notes: The spontaneous use is limited to verbs of mind and feeling, like 「思う・感じる・偲ぶ・案じる・悔やむ・待つ・思い出す」.
It looks the same as the passive, potential, and honorific forms, so rely on context: 「昔が思い出される」 is spontaneous, 「人に悪く思われる」 is passive.
Potential forms like 「泣ける」 and 「笑える」 can also mean "makes you want to cry / laugh," as in 「この映画は泣ける」.

daily.title: Visiting your hometown
daily.description: Back home, old memories return.
daily.example: Walking down this road, my school days come back to me.

daily.title: Reading an essay
daily.description: An essay describes the change of seasons.
daily.example: In the coolness of morning and evening, you can feel autumn arriving.

daily.title: Worrying about family
daily.description: Writing a letter to parents far away.
daily.example: As the cold grows harsher, I find myself worrying about my parents' health.

work.title: News report
work.description: A report speculates on the cause of an incident.
work.example: The fire is believed to have been caused by an electrical fault.

work.title: Academic paper
work.description: A paper states a conclusion cautiously.
work.example: From the above results, it can be considered that the two are correlated.

etymology: 「れる・られる」 come from the classical auxiliaries 「る・らる」, whose core meaning was "to come about naturally" (spontaneity). The passive, potential, and honorific uses are generally thought to have developed from this.

similar.title: 〜れる・〜られる (passive)
similar.explanation: The passive has an agent (先生に叱られる). The spontaneous form has no agent; the feeling just arises (昔が思い出される).

similar.title: 〜させられる (can't help but ...)
similar.explanation: 「考えさせられる」 stresses being moved by something and having to think, with a clear trigger. Spontaneous 「思われる」 stresses the feeling arising on its own.

similar.title: 〜と考えられる
similar.explanation: 「〜と考えられる」 is a set spontaneous phrase for judgments, common in papers. This entry is the general overview of the spontaneous use.

similar.title: 〜ずにはいられない
similar.explanation: 「〜ずにはいられない」 means "can't help doing an action." The spontaneous form means a feeling or sensation arises naturally, not necessarily an action.

title: 〜させられる (can't help but ...)
meaning: Formally the causative-passive, but it doesn't mean "be made to do." It means being moved by something so that you "can't help but ...".
connection: Verb causative-passive form (考えさせられる, 感心させられる, 驚かされる)

senses.label: Makes you think
senses.meaning: Moved by a work or someone's words and actions, you can't help thinking, reflecting, or realizing. Common: 「考えさせられる」, 「反省させられる」, 「気づかされる」.
senses.connection: Noun + に（は）+ 考えさせられる／反省させられる／気づかされる
examples: This movie really made me think about what family means.
My child's honest words made me realize something important.
His sincere attitude often makes me reflect on myself.

senses.label: Can't help admiring
senses.meaning: Shows involuntary admiration or amazement at someone's ability or performance. Common: 「感心させられる」, 「驚かされる」, 「唸らされる」.
senses.connection: Noun + に（は）+ 感心させられる／驚かされる／唸らされる
examples: I'm always impressed by how hard he works.
I was amazed at how advanced the technology was.
The veteran actor's superb performance left me in awe.

senses.label: Painfully aware
senses.meaning: Through an experience, you become keenly aware of something, usually your own shortcomings or a harsh reality. Common: 「思い知らされる」, 「痛感させられる」.
senses.connection: Noun + を + 思い知らされる／痛感させられる
examples: This failure made me painfully aware of my own inexperience.
Every disaster brings home how important it is to be prepared.

notes: The subject is "I" (the speaker), usually omitted. The thing that moves you is marked with 「に（は）」.
「親に掃除をさせられた」 ("my parents made me clean") is an ordinary causative-passive meaning being forced. That is not this usage.
Godan verbs often use the short form 「〜される」: 「驚かされる」, 「気づかされる」, 「思い知らされる」.

daily.title: After a documentary
daily.description: Sharing thoughts with a friend after watching a documentary.
daily.example: That documentary really gave me a lot to think about.

daily.title: Praising a friend
daily.description: Your friend's cooking is excellent.
daily.example: Your cooking skills never fail to amaze me.

work.title: Meeting wrap-up
work.description: A department head sums up customer feedback in a meeting.
work.example: The survey results gave us a lot to reflect on.

work.title: Thank-you letter
work.description: Thanking a business partner and praising their professionalism.
work.example: We are always impressed by the meticulous work of your company.

work.title: Book review
work.description: Evaluating a book in a review.
work.example: This is a book that makes you painfully aware, once again, of the problems of modern society.

etymology: Made from causative 「させる」 plus passive 「られる」, literally "to be made to ... (by something)." The trigger is treated as the "causer" and you as the one affected, which creates the spontaneous sense of "can't help but ...".

similar.title: 〜させられる (causative-passive)
similar.explanation: The ordinary causative-passive means being forced to do something unwanted (残業させられる). This usage is about being moved emotionally, with no sense of force or complaint.

similar.title: 〜れる・〜られる (spontaneous)
similar.explanation: Spontaneous 「思い出される」 is a feeling arising on its own. 「考えさせられる」 stresses that something outside moved you.

similar.title: 〜ずにはいられない
similar.explanation: 「感心せずにはいられない」 stresses a subjective urge you can't hold back. 「感心させられる」 stresses being moved by the other party; it's more objective and understated.

title: 〜か (rhetorical question / strong denial)
meaning: Sentence-final 「か」 here is not a real question. It uses a rhetorical question to strongly deny: "As if ...!" "Could ... possibly be? (No way.)"
connection: Verb/adjective plain form + か; verb volitional / conjectural form + か (〜（よ）うか, 〜だろうか)

senses.label: As if ...!
senses.meaning: Said with falling intonation in speech to strongly deny or refuse: "No way I'd ...!" Often paired with 「誰が」 or 「そんなこと」. Rough in tone, mostly used by men.
senses.connection: Plain form + か (！) (誰が信じるか, 知るか)
examples: Who'd believe a story like that!
How should I know!
As if I'd lose to a guy like that!

senses.label: Could it possibly ...?
senses.meaning: In writing, 「〜（よ）うか」, 「〜だろうか」, 「〜であろうか」 ask rhetorically, "Could ... ever be? (Never.)" Solemn in tone; common in essays and speeches.
senses.connection: Verb volitional / conjectural form + か (あろうか, 言えようか, 〜だろうか)
examples: Could there be any greater joy than this?
Who could blame him?
Is it really all right to just leave it like this?

notes: Spoken 「〜か！」 is very blunt. Don't use it with elders or in formal settings.
The same sentence with rising intonation is an ordinary question. Rhetorical meaning depends on falling intonation and context.
More common strong-denial forms are 「〜ものか」 and 「〜もんか」, which are a bit softer than bare 「か」.

daily.title: Bickering with a friend
daily.description: A friend jokes that you'll lose, and you won't accept it.
daily.example: As if I'd lose to you!

daily.title: Refusing an unreasonable request
daily.description: Someone makes an outrageous demand, and you angrily refuse.
daily.example: As if I'd do something like that!

daily.title: Reading a novel
daily.description: A character expresses deep emotion.
daily.example: Could there be any greater happiness in this world?

work.title: Speech
work.description: A politician stresses how serious a problem is.
work.example: Can we really stand by in silence and let a situation like this pass?

work.title: Editorial
work.description: A newspaper editorial criticizes the government.
work.example: How could this possibly win the public's understanding?

etymology: 「か」 is originally a sentence-final particle for questions. Asking a question when the answer is obvious amounts to saying "of course not," which gave rise to rhetorical questions and strong denial. In classical Japanese, 「〜やは」 and 「〜かは」 worked the same way.

similar.title: 〜ものか・〜もんか
similar.explanation: 「〜ものか」 is specifically for strong denial and resolve, so the meaning is clear. Bare 「〜か」 is rougher and more direct, and relies more on intonation.

similar.title: 〜てたまるか
similar.explanation: 「負けてたまるか」 means "I absolutely won't let ...," stressing you won't stand for it. 「負けるか」 just means "As if I'd lose," with slightly less resolve.

similar.title: 〜のだろうか
similar.explanation: 「〜のだろうか」 can be a simple question or self-question. It's rhetorical only when a negative answer is clearly expected.

title: 〜てやる (fierce resolve)
meaning: Not "doing something for someone," but the speaker's fierce resolve: "I'll ... no matter what!" "Just watch me ...!" Often with resentment toward or defiance of others.
connection: Verb te-form + やる (やるぞ／やるからな／やろうじゃないか)

senses.label: I'll ... no matter what
senses.meaning: Strong determination, often with a sense of "I'll show those who looked down on me." Often said to yourself. Pairs with 「絶対に」, 「必ず」, 「いつか」.
senses.connection: Verb te-form + やる (ぞ) (合格してやる, 見返してやる)
examples: I'm going to pass the next exam, no matter what!
Someday I'll show those guys who made fun of me.
I'll grab the championship with my own hands!

senses.label: Just watch me ...
senses.meaning: Driven by anger or frustration, you vow to do something that hurts the other person or burns bridges. Very intense, often with an exclamation mark.
senses.connection: Verb te-form + やる (！)／やるからな (辞めてやる, 訴えてやる)
examples: I'm quitting this lousy company right now!
Remember this. I'll get you back for it.
I can't keep quiet any longer. I'm going to sue.

senses.label: Bring it on
senses.meaning: 「〜てやろうじゃないか」 means accepting a challenge and going all in: "Then I'll show you." Firm and defiant.
senses.connection: Verb te-form + やろうじゃないか
examples: If you're going to say that much, then I'll do it and show you.
Interesting. I accept your challenge.

notes: Rough and emotional. Don't use it to an elder's or a boss's face.
「弟に本を読んでやる」 is the giving-and-receiving use, "do something for a junior." This entry is different: there's no beneficiary, only the speaker's will.
Often appears with 「ぞ」, 「からな」, or 「！」. In writing, mostly in novel and manga dialogue.

daily.title: After being looked down on
daily.description: After friends laugh at you, you make a silent vow.
daily.example: Just you wait. I'm going to lose weight no matter what!

daily.title: Losing at a game
daily.description: You lose several rounds in a row and refuse to give up.
daily.example: One more round! This time I'm going to win!

daily.title: Reading manga
daily.description: The main character makes a vow.
daily.example: I'm going to become King of the Pirates!

work.title: Venting with a coworker
work.description: After a harsh scolding from the boss, you vent to a colleague. Only among close colleagues.
work.example: Just watch. I'm going to be number one next quarter, no matter what.

etymology: 「やる」 originally means "to give, to send off." 「〜てやる」 was for doing something for a junior or subordinate. Because the speaker imposes their action on the other person from above, it developed the defiant use "I'll do it anyway, I'll show you."

similar.title: 〜てやる
similar.explanation: The N4 「〜てやる」 is giving and receiving: doing something for a junior or an animal (犬に餌をやる). This entry has no beneficiary and expresses resolve or revenge.

similar.title: 〜てみせる
similar.explanation: 「〜てみせる」 means "I'll do it and prove it," stressing proof to others, and is a bit more positive. 「〜てやる」 is rougher, often with anger or a wish for revenge.

similar.title: 〜ものか
similar.explanation: 「負けるものか」 expresses resolve through a negative rhetorical question ("I'll never ..."). 「勝ってやる」 expresses resolve in the affirmative ("I will ...").
